summary:
Recommendation: move the wordpress MySQL database to three AWS services in three waves. Wave 1 moves it to Aurora MySQL, which ends up serving 63.6% of the queries; wave 2 puts ElastiCache in front of 19 hot reads (82.1% of calls); wave 3 moves 36.4% of the queries to DynamoDB. The projected cost of the full modernization is $507 per month at AWS Price List on-demand prices for us-east-1, retrieved 2026-10-25. No current cost was collected for the source database, so the plan claims no saving against it.

Risk: overall risk is medium. The main exposures are the tables kept in sync by change data capture (CDC) and the queries where two engines scored almost the same: test the CDC replication and confirm where those queries run before wave 3 starts.

Decision: approve wave 1. It is safe to approve: it moves the database 1:1 to Aurora MySQL, the same engine family as MySQL, with its current data model, and its cutover waits until schema and data parity is validated against the source.
summary_deterministic: Analyzed 50 source tables and 107 query patterns across 3 target database(s). Workload split: Aurora MySQL handles 68 queries (63.6%), DynamoDB handles 39 queries (36.4%). Cache layer: ElastiCache fronts 19 designed cached reads (82.1% of calls) cache-aside and owns no queries. Schema design produced 54 target objects: 107 queries in 60 query groups; 119 in-scope access patterns (Aurora MySQL: 20 target tables, 68 in-scope access patterns; DynamoDB: 17 target tables, 34 in-scope access patterns; ElastiCache: 17 key designs, 17 in-scope access patterns). The schema design's table map lists 22 source tables (Aurora MySQL, DynamoDB, ElastiCache). Estimated monthly cost: $507.39. 9 open migration risks (overall: MEDIUM); 5 more were resolved by the assignment. Top query groups by throughput: Option reads, Post reads, API key writes. Other targets evaluated: DocumentDB (consolidated into Aurora MySQL by the reality check), OpenSearch (consolidated into Aurora MySQL by the reality check).

risks.description: [dynamodb] Wave 3: 57 queries read 16 tables on an engine that does not own them. 53 of them read a copy of 13 tables that CDC keeps in sync from DynamoDB across 1 engine pair, so a read there can miss a recent write. The other 3 tables are written by no captured query, so a one-time copy serves them.
risks.mitigation: Before Wave 3 starts, set up CDC for each engine pair the sources of truth section lists, and send any read that must see its own write to its source of truth; copy the read-only tables once and confirm nothing outside the captured workload writes them. Compare the row counts on both sides at the Wave 3 gate.

risks.description: [dynamodb] Wave 3: 19 queries were decided by less than 5 points, and 5 more were exact ties a routing rule settled: Aurora MySQL keeps 14 close calls and 5 ties over DynamoDB; DynamoDB takes 5 close calls over Aurora MySQL. A small change in the scores moves them.

risks.description: [elasticache] The cache design marks 1 pattern unsupported; the engineering report lists each one with its workaround under Target schemas by engine.
details: unsupported pattern: This is the slug uniqueness check WordPress runs while saving a post. wp_posts has no unique index on (post_type, post_name), so this query is the only thing preventing duplicate slugs. A cache hit that missed a concurrent insert or a failed delete would produce duplicate slugs and URL collisions. The query runs only on post save (2.7 calls per second), so caching it saves little load. Workaround: Run the check on Aurora MySQL against the existing post_name index, inside the post save path. The cache does not hold or answer slug lookups
risks.mitigation: Serve this pattern from its owner engine or add it to the cache design before the Wave 2 gate, as the design's workaround for each says.

risks.description: [aurora_mysql] 19 source objects need application code on Aurora MySQL: 17 column defaults; 1 sql calc found rows; 1 zero date default. The schema carries them over without the database logic.
risks.mitigation: Move the logic of each one into the application before the Wave 1 gate, as the schema design's note for it says.

risks.description: [aurora_mysql] The Aurora MySQL schema design records 10 trade-offs to review, listed under Migration trade-offs in the engineering report.
details: After cutover, confirm with EXPLAIN that the optimizer picks the new composites (post_id_meta_key, order_item_id_meta_key, hook_group_status_claim) and not the older single-column or hook_status_scheduled_date_gmt indexes. Run ANALYZE TABLE after the bulk load so the statistics are current
Aurora MySQL design trade-off

Composite indexes are added on wp_postmeta (post_id, meta_key) and wp_woocommerce_order_itemmeta (order_item_id, meta_key), and on wp_actionscheduler_actions (hook, group_id, status, claim_id). The single-column indexes stay because they return rows already ordered by meta_id for the per-object meta loads
Index builds on wp_postmeta (about 449,000 rows) and wp_woocommerce_order_itemmeta (about 244,000 rows) are small. Create the indexes after the bulk load, not before, to shorten load time

Query `2389b8a0` (wp_terms join wp_term_taxonomy by term_id IN, about 2 calls/s) recorded about 11,800 full table scans and is not covered by this delta. The term tables are small and the query averages 0.29 ms, so this is not a blocker, but check that the term_taxonomy index on (term_id, taxonomy) came across in the carried-over DDL

Query `a0b655ea` (911 ms, about 369,000 rows examined) still aggregates many postmeta rows even with the composite index. The replica keeps that load off the storefront, and moving to WooCommerce HPOS / wc_order_stats-based analytics is the long-term fix at the application layer

Report-to-replica routing: the WooCommerce Analytics/report queries (`a0b655ea`, `fc99562b`, `cb3300c6`, `d99618ea`, `119b7fbf`) are read-only. Check that the HyperDB or LudicrousDB rules send only those queries to the reader endpoint, and that admin write paths and read-after-write flows such as checkout and order status changes stay on the writer

Reporting queries go to an Aurora Replica through the reader endpoint, and repeated option, meta and term reads go to an ElastiCache object cache. The schema stays a 1:1 carry-over of the WordPress and WooCommerce tables

The source index type_status_date leads with ID, so it cannot serve filters on post_type and post_status. The target redefines it as (post_type, post_status, post_date, ID), the column order WordPress core defines
Zero dates are carried over unchanged under a load-session `sql_mode` that accepts them, and are not replaced with real dates or NULL in the NOT NULL WordPress columns
risks.mitigation: Review these trade-offs with the team that builds Aurora MySQL before Wave 1 starts, and test each one the application depends on.

risks.description: [dynamodb] The DynamoDB schema design records 41 trade-offs to review, listed under Migration trade-offs in the engineering report.
details: API key authentication by consumer_key (query `1794daed`) reads the ApiKeysByConsumerKey GSI with an INCLUDE projection of user_id, permissions, consumer_secret, nonces and last_access, so the lookup needs no base-table fetch

About 72% of DDB-AP-30 calls and 92% of DDB-AP-31 calls return no item, but each miss still costs 0.5 read unit. A caching layer in front of option reads that also caches misses (as WordPress object caching already does) would cut both cost and the load on any single key
Auto-increment ids (comment_ID, log_id, meta_id) have no DynamoDB equivalent; the application generates them (a time-ordered numeric id) and writes with attribute_not_exists on the key

Cost, WpPostmeta writes: about 260 write units per second is roughly $440/month on-demand at the 1,619-byte schema-rule size. Measured rows average 144 bytes, which would be 1 write unit each. Check the real item sizes after the first load before choosing provisioned capacity

Cost, WpPosts reads: about 470 read units per second is roughly $150/month on-demand. Consider provisioned capacity with auto-scaling once the traffic shape is known. If posts are read far more often than they change, consider caching hot posts

Cost, WpPosts writes: the comment_count UpdateItem is billed at 8 write units because the item is 7,526 bytes. At 167.6 write units per second, on-demand cost is roughly $270/month for one counter. The measured average post row is about 711 bytes, so the real bill may be about 1 write unit per update. If the large figure holds after migration, move comment_count to a small separate counter item (for example a WpPostCounters table keyed by id, or a sort-key split). That cuts the cost by about 8x

Cost: on demand at design load, reads come to about 1,289 read units/s (~3.3B a month) and writes to about 258 write units/s (~670M a month). That is several hundred dollars a month, well over the $100 per-table threshold. Traffic is steady key-value traffic, so the team should compare provisioned capacity with auto scaling (or reserved capacity) against on-demand pricing

DDB-AP-1 describes two sources for the throttle's last-written last_access: ElastiCache and the ApiKeysByConsumerKey projection. Each authenticated request already reads the projection (DDB-AP-3), so the ElastiCache copy looks redundant. Document one source of truth, or drop the cache dependency, to avoid running an extra store for this check

DDB-AP-27: the design says the source guard `(SELECT ? FROM DUAL) IS NULL` binds a value the application already computed. If the real production statement is Action Scheduler's 'unique action' subquery (no pending or in-progress action with the same hook, args and group), a check in the application is a race. That would need a sentinel item keyed by hook#args_hash#group, written in a TransactWriteItems with attribute_not_exists and deleted when the action completes. Confirm the guard's real form before cutover
DDB-AP-29 (query `3440484f`): a GetItem plus a client-side post_type check costs the same as a Query with a FilterExpression, and keeps the code path the same as DDB-AP-12. This is optional

DDB-AP-33 (add_option, ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE): an unconditional PutItem replaces the whole item, so upserting an existing option drops its migrated option_id. MySQL's ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE only touches the listed columns. If option_id lineage matters, use UpdateItem SET option_value, autoload (it upserts too) instead of PutItem. No in-scope query reads option_id, so this is optional

DDB-AP-34 covers transient expiry deletes. Writing a TTL epoch attribute on transient options (_transient_* / _transient_timeout_*) would let DynamoDB delete expired transients with no write capacity charge, which takes part of the 24 deletes/s off the bill. Reads must still check expiry, because TTL deletion can lag
DynamoDB has no AUTO_INCREMENT, so the application generates ID, meta_id, umeta_id, order_item_id and action_id before each insert, and every insert carries attribute_not_exists on its key

DynamoDB has no server-side COUNT, so the approved-comment count per post (query `8c66eaee`) is served in scope by a KEYS_ONLY GSI CommentsByPostApproval (comment_post_id, comment_approved) queried with Select=COUNT instead of a maintained counter item

MySQL reports 0 affected rows when an UPDATE sets a value identical to the current one. DynamoDB's conditional UpdateItem succeeds in that case. Callers that branch on the affected-row count should not depend on that MySQL behavior
No index on autoload is created, because no in-scope query filters on it; the source's autoload index is dropped

Only part of each table's attributes is listed (_attrs_sampled on WpComments, WpWcProductMetaLookup and WpWoocommerceDownloadableProductPermissions). Before migration, confirm that comment_approved (the GSI sort key) and user_id/user_email (set by DDB-AP-10) are mapped in the full attribute list
Option reads use eventually consistent GetItem at 0.5 read unit per item, which keeps the read load at 1,289 read units per second at design rate
Order items are stored under their order (partition key order_id, sort key order_item_id), and order item meta under its order_item_id

Post and meta values larger than 400 KB: the application-side S3 offload described in the trade-offs needs a defined pointer attribute name and a migration-time check for oversized post_content and meta_value rows

Post meta, order item meta and term meta each become a table keyed by the parent id with a composite sort key `{meta_key}#{meta_id}`, so an update by parent id and meta key is a Query on the key prefix followed by one UpdateItem per matching item
Posts and post meta stay separate tables even though the analysis groups them, because no in-scope query reads them together: post reads fetch only wp_posts rows and post meta traffic is writes only

Reserved stock and download permissions are keyed by order_id with the product_id or permission_id as sort key, so the delete by order (query `77cd1ad7`) and the customer reassignment by order (query `2264704d`) read their items by key
TEXT and LONGTEXT columns (comment_content, message, meta_value, nonces) stay inline as string attributes
TEXT and LONGTEXT columns stay inline: wp_posts averages 711 bytes per row, wp_actionscheduler_actions 587 bytes, wp_postmeta 144 bytes and order item meta 131 bytes, against the 400 KB item limit

The Action Scheduler queue runner (claiming due actions by status and scheduled_date_gmt) is not in the captured workload. When it moves over, it will need an index whose partition key is not the low-cardinality status alone, for example a write-sharded status#shard key with scheduled_date_gmt as sort key

The WpUsers partition holds 1 user and 21 meta rows, so all user reads hit one key at 128.5 read units per second. That is fine at 4.3% of the per-partition limit, but recheck it if the site adds many logged-in users and read traffic grows a lot
The comment meta read with an IN list of comment ids (query `65f7884e`) becomes one Query per comment id on the comment's item collection, issued in parallel
The comment_count update rewrites a post item sized at 7,526 bytes by the schema rule, which bills 8 write units per update, 167.6 write units per second at design load
The full table scan of tax rate classes (query `329367a2`, 37.9 reads per second) becomes one Query on a single TAX_RATE_CLASS item collection whose sort key is the class name followed by its id

The hot-partition check assumes the whole read load lands on one option name: 1,289 read units per second is 43% of the 3,000 per-key limit, and 258 write units per second is 25.8% of the 1,000 per-key limit
The key-scoped term meta update (query `3c5c8a79`) names term_id and meta_key; term_id is the partition key and meta_key leads the sort key, rather than a separate partition key on meta_key

The last_access update (query `0452bed2`, 248.3 calls per second at design load, 46.68% lock time in MySQL) is throttled in the application: it writes only when the key's last written last_access is more than 60 s old, using the per-key value cached in ElastiCache and the last_access now projected into ApiKeysByConsumerKey
The post lookup by ID and post_type (query `3440484f`) is a Query on the post key with a FilterExpression on post_type
The scheduled action insert's `WHERE (SELECT ? FROM DUAL) IS NULL` guard carries a value the application computed beforehand, so the application evaluates it before issuing the PutItem
The table is keyed by option_name instead of the auto-increment option_id, because every in-scope read and write addresses an option by name
WpWcProductMetaLookup.sku is not unique in WooCommerce (it has a non-unique index), so not writing a sentinel is correct. Revisit this only if the business makes SKU uniqueness a rule

WpWcTaxRateClasses uses a constant partition key. That is fine at 2 items and 37.9 RPS. If tax class reads grow by orders of magnitude, cache the list in the application rather than sharding the partition
log_date_gmt is formatted with a 'Z' suffix but log_date_local is not. This is intentional and correct, but downstream consumers should know about it

option_value (LONGTEXT) stays inline in the item: the measured average row is 360 bytes against the 400 KB item limit, and capacity is sized on the 1,283-byte schema estimate that counts the column at 1 KB

risks.description: [elasticache] The ElastiCache schema design records 18 trade-offs to review, listed under Migration trade-offs in the engineering report.
details: Action scheduler reads use a 60-second TTL because the scheduler's status, claim and attempt updates are absent from the captured write set. Hook lookups cache only two fixed status sets and at most 1,000 actions per hook, with zero-padded members so equal scores sort by numeric action_id

Both the fill script and EXPIRE NX need Redis OSS 7.0+ or Valkey 7.2+. Pin the engine version in IaC. Also keep every value in the fill JSON as a JSON string, because Lua number-to-integer conversion would truncate a value like 19.99
Child and title lookups on wp_posts store only post IDs, cached per parent or per type and title. Empty results are cached too, because the child and title queries return 0 rows on average
Every read-then-fill key has a version key in its slot. Fills go through a Lua compare-and-set script, and writers bump the version in the same transaction that deletes the data keys
Hash field order does not follow meta_id or order_item_id, so the client sorts the HGETALL result numerically to match the ORDER BY of the source queries
Hashes that cache one field per query variant set their TTL only on the first fill (EXPIRE NX). Termmeta-ordered term lists carry a global termmeta version in the field name

In cluster mode, IN-list reads (EC-AP-2, EC-AP-3, EC-AP-14) span slots. The client has to use a cluster-aware pipeline that splits commands by slot. The Aurora fill must read each missing entity's `:ver` before the single owner query

Key counts in the key designs are already 10x today's rows: 11,990 posts become 119,900 post keys, 23,163 options become 231,630 option keys and 24,713 order items become 247,130 item meta keys. At that 10x volume the cache holds about 1.7 million data keys plus about 0.5 million version keys and about 1.4 GB of values. Adding per-key overhead of about 90 B (about 0.2 GB) and hashtable encoding for meta hashes whose JSON values exceed the 64 B hash-max-listpack-value (about 0.7 GB) gives about 2.3 GB
Key patterns use literal hash tags. The braces in wp_postmeta:{post_id} hold the actual post_id, so a data key, its :keys companion, its :ver key and its :lock key share one slot

Numeric IDs share hash tags across tables: `wp_posts:{1842}`, `wp_postmeta:{1842}`, `wp_term_relationships:{1842}` and `wp_actionscheduler_actions:{1842}` all land in the same slot. That is harmless for overall distribution, but a viral product concentrates all of its keys on one shard. Watch per-shard EngineCPUUtilization

Option lookups by name are cached with negative entries. Query `66c96f95` returns a row on 28% of calls and query `e223aefb` on 8%, so a missing option is stored as __missing=1 instead of being skipped
Post meta is cached per post as one hash, plus a second hash from meta_key to meta_id. Both are filled by one atomic script from one owner read, and any meta write deletes both
Tax rate classes (2 rows) are one pre-sorted JSON string with a 24-hour TTL, and no captured write covers the table
The object-term joins (queries `d5ae7abb` and `4481cc0c`) are pre-joined into a term_id list per object, and the term rows are stored separately in wp_terms:{term_id}
The slug uniqueness check, query `fcfd82fa`, stays on Aurora MySQL and is not cached
Values over 100 KB are cached as an __oversize=1 marker with the normal TTL instead of being skipped, and autoloaded options are held in the PHP process for 5 seconds

WooCommerce order items and item meta are cached per order and per item, with a meta_key-to-meta_id companion hash for existence checks. Invalidation also covers item updates, item deletes and meta deletes made outside the captured workload
`wp_termmeta:ver` is a single global key read on every termmeta-ordered request. Its traffic is low, and the 5-second in-process option cache pattern could be applied to it if it gets hot

optimizations.rationale: Query `12f856ea` filters `post_type = ? AND post_status != ? AND post_status != ?` and sorts by post_date DESC, ID. The `!=` predicates make post_status a range, so the corrected type_status_date index narrows the scan to one post_type but cannot supply the post_date order: a filesort remains, and `SQL_CALC_FOUND_ROWS` still counts every matching row. trade_offs.description: The source index type_status_date leads with ID, so it cannot serve filters on post_type and post_status. The target redefines it as (post_type, post_status, post_date, ID), the column order WordPress core defines.
trade_offs.impact: Listings with equality on post type and status (queries `305e3eaa`, `d4bf16d6`) read only the matching rows in post_date order. Query `12f856ea` excludes statuses with `!=`, so it still scans every row of its post type and sorts them: rows examined drop from about 15,790 per call to about the row count of that post type, and a filesort remains. No application change is needed; the index name stays the same.

trade_offs.description: Composite indexes are added on wp_postmeta (post_id, meta_key) and wp_woocommerce_order_itemmeta (order_item_id, meta_key), and on wp_actionscheduler_actions (hook, group_id, status, claim_id). The single-column indexes stay because they return rows already ordered by meta_id for the per-object meta loads.
trade_offs.impact: Meta lookups by object and key read one row instead of 10 to 19 rows, and the WooCommerce sales reports join meta by key without scanning. Each insert into these tables maintains one more index, which costs little at the observed near-zero write rate. Storage grows by a few tens of MB.

trade_offs.description: Reporting queries go to an Aurora Replica through the reader endpoint, and repeated option, meta and term reads go to an ElastiCache object cache. The schema stays a 1:1 carry-over of the WordPress and WooCommerce tables.
trade_offs.impact: Report results on the replica can trail the writer by up to about 100 ms of replica lag, which does not affect sales totals shown in dashboards. Keeping the WordPress schema unchanged means plugins and core upgrades keep working with no code changes.

trade_offs.description: Zero dates are carried over unchanged under a load-session `sql_mode` that accepts them, and are not replaced with real dates or NULL in the NOT NULL WordPress columns.
trade_offs.impact: Drafts keep their floating publish dates and WordPress behaves after cutover exactly as before. The target keeps holding zero dates, because WordPress removes the zero-date and strict modes from its own sessions, so reporting or ETL tools that read these columns must handle '0000-00-00 00:00:00'.

trade_offs.impact: DynamoDB receives at most one write per API key per 60 s, bounded at 3.88 writes per second table-wide (the 1.56% of source calls that change a row) for 7.76 WCU/s instead of 496.6 WCU/s, a 64x cut that also removes the single-item worst case (0.8% of one partition's write limit instead of 49.7%). Because last_access is now projected, each real write also writes ApiKeysByConsumerKey once (7.76 WCU/s), which stays rare under the throttle. The access pattern keeps the 248.3 calls per second as its design rate because that is the measured call rate; the hot partition entries carry the throttled write rate. Row-lock waits disappear because each DynamoDB write is atomic per item, and last_access is at most 60 s behind the latest request, matching the source where 98% of updates change no row.

trade_offs.description: API key authentication by consumer_key (query `1794daed`) reads the ApiKeysByConsumerKey GSI with an INCLUDE projection of user_id, permissions, consumer_secret, nonces and last_access, so the lookup needs no base-table fetch.
trade_offs.impact: ApiKeysByConsumerKey lags the WpWoocommerceApiKeys table until DynamoDB applies each write to it; a request using a key created in that window fails authentication, and the key-creation flow that must use the key at once reads the base item by key_id with a strongly consistent GetItem. consumer_key is not unique in the source, so no uniqueness sentinel is written.

trade_offs.description: The full table scan of tax rate classes (query `329367a2`, 37.9 reads per second) becomes one Query on a single TAX_RATE_CLASS item collection whose sort key is the class name followed by its id.
trade_offs.impact: The 2-item list comes back in name order from one partition for 18.95 RCU/s, 0.6% of the partition limit. The unique slug is set only by the migration (no in-scope write changes it), so no sentinel item is needed; an admin flow that adds classes later writes a slug sentinel with attribute_not_exists in the same transaction. ElastiCache can hold the list if read volume grows further.

trade_offs.description: DynamoDB has no server-side COUNT, so the approved-comment count per post (query `8c66eaee`) is served in scope by a KEYS_ONLY GSI CommentsByPostApproval (comment_post_id, comment_approved) queried with Select=COUNT instead of a maintained counter item.
trade_offs.impact: Each count reads every matching index entry; the source examines 2.4 rows per call, so a count reads 2.4 index entries for 0.5 RCU. A counter item was not chosen because approval status changes happen in writes outside this workload, and a counter updated only on insert would drift. comment_approved is a mutable GSI key: each moderation change deletes and reinserts the index entry (2 index writes of 77 bytes). The count lags new comments until DynamoDB applies the write to the index.

trade_offs.description: Reserved stock and download permissions are keyed by order_id with the product_id or permission_id as sort key, so the delete by order (query `77cd1ad7`) and the customer reassignment by order (query `2264704d`) read their items by key.
trade_offs.impact: Each set-based statement becomes a Query on the order's items followed by a BatchWriteItem of deletes or one UpdateItem per permission. These are not atomic across items: a failed item is retried by the application, and both operations are idempotent, so a retry is safe.

trade_offs.description: Auto-increment ids (comment_ID, log_id, meta_id) have no DynamoDB equivalent; the application generates them (a time-ordered numeric id) and writes with attribute_not_exists on the key.
trade_offs.impact: Inserts no longer depend on a central sequence. Action scheduler logs are grouped per action_id with log_id as sort key, so the log of one action reads in time order.

trade_offs.description: TEXT and LONGTEXT columns (comment_content, message, meta_value, nonces) stay inline as string attributes.
trade_offs.impact: Measured average rows are 552 bytes for wp_comments and 168 bytes for wp_actionscheduler_logs against the 400 KB item limit. wp_commentmeta and wp_woocommerce_api_keys hold 0 rows, so their 52,429-byte averages are the empty-table allocation, not stored values; the write path stores any single value above 350 KB in S3 and keeps a pointer attribute instead.

trade_offs.description: The comment meta read with an IN list of comment ids (query `65f7884e`) becomes one Query per comment id on the comment's item collection, issued in parallel.
trade_offs.impact: Each comment's metadata returns in meta_id order, matching the source ORDER BY; results across comments are merged in the application in the order the ids were requested.

Document one source of truth, or drop the cache dependency, to avoid running an extra store for this check.

trade_offs.description: Post meta, order item meta and term meta each become a table keyed by the parent id with a composite sort key `{meta_key}#{meta_id}`, so an update by parent id and meta key is a Query on the key prefix followed by one UpdateItem per matching item.
trade_offs.impact: The single SQL UPDATE becomes two calls in the application (find the keys, then update them); WordPress allows repeated meta keys per parent, and the meta_id suffix keeps each row a separate item. The Query reads one item on average (rows_affected about 1).

trade_offs.description: The key-scoped term meta update (query `3c5c8a79`) names term_id and meta_key; term_id is the partition key and meta_key leads the sort key, rather than a separate partition key on meta_key.
trade_offs.impact: meta_key has unknown cardinality and a small set of repeated values, so a partition key on it alone would concentrate writes on few values. Every in-scope term meta read and write pins term_id, so no GSI is needed. The source full table scan of query `50b46567` becomes one Query per term_id in its IN list.

trade_offs.description: wp_users and wp_usermeta share one item collection in WpUsers keyed by user_id, with the profile under sort key PROFILE and each meta row under META#<zero-padded umeta_id>.
trade_offs.impact: The profile lookup is a GetItem and the meta load is one Query per user that returns rows already in umeta_id order. The site has 1 user and 21 meta rows, so all user reads land on one partition at 128.5 read units per second at design load, 4.3% of the per-partition limit.

trade_offs.description: Posts and post meta stay separate tables even though the analysis groups them, because no in-scope query reads them together: post reads fetch only wp_posts rows and post meta traffic is writes only.
trade_offs.impact: Post meta writes (about 260 write units per second at design load) scale on their own table without touching post items. A future page render that needs a post and its meta issues a GetItem plus a Query.

trade_offs.description: Order items are stored under their order (partition key order_id, sort key order_item_id), and order item meta under its order_item_id.
trade_offs.impact: Listing an order's items is a single Query on order_id. Order item meta writes address their parent by order_item_id, which they already carry.

trade_offs.description: DynamoDB has no AUTO_INCREMENT, so the application generates ID, meta_id, umeta_id, order_item_id and action_id before each insert, and every insert carries attribute_not_exists on its key.
trade_offs.impact: An id generator (a counter item updated with an atomic ADD, or a time-ordered unique id) replaces the database sequence. The conditional put rejects a duplicate id instead of overwriting an existing row.

trade_offs.description: TEXT and LONGTEXT columns stay inline: wp_posts averages 711 bytes per row, wp_actionscheduler_actions 587 bytes, wp_postmeta 144 bytes and order item meta 131 bytes, against the 400 KB item limit.
trade_offs.impact: No S3 offload is needed for current content. wp_usermeta (16,478 bytes measured over 21 rows) and wp_termmeta (0 rows) report averages dominated by page overhead; a single meta_value or post_content above 400 KB fails the write, and the application moves such a value to S3 with a pointer attribute.

trade_offs.description: The comment_count update rewrites a post item sized at 7,526 bytes by the schema rule, which bills 8 write units per update, 167.6 write units per second at design load.
trade_offs.impact: Writing one counter costs as much as writing the whole post. The figure stays at 19.1% of the per-partition write limit, so the counter stays on the post item.

trade_offs.description: The scheduled action insert's `WHERE (SELECT ? FROM DUAL) IS NULL` guard carries a value the application computed beforehand, so the application evaluates it before issuing the PutItem.
trade_offs.impact: No in-scope query reads actions by hook, status or schedule date, so WpActionschedulerActions has no GSI. A queue runner that claims due actions by status and date needs an index added when that read moves to DynamoDB.

trade_offs.description: The post lookup by ID and post_type (query `3440484f`) is a Query on the post key with a FilterExpression on post_type.
trade_offs.impact: At most one item matches the key, so the filter reads one item and returns it or nothing; no index on post_type is needed.

trade_offs.description: [PE note] Cost, WpPosts writes: the comment_count UpdateItem is billed at 8 write units because the item is 7,526 bytes. At 167.6 write units per second, on-demand cost is roughly $270/month for one counter. The measured average post row is about 711 bytes, so the real bill may be about 1 write unit per update. If the large figure holds after migration, move comment_count to a small separate counter item (for example a WpPostCounters table keyed by id, or a sort-key split). That cuts the cost by about 8x.

trade_offs.description: The table is keyed by option_name instead of the auto-increment option_id, because every in-scope read and write addresses an option by name.
trade_offs.impact: Every query becomes a single-item GetItem, PutItem, UpdateItem or DeleteItem. The unique index on option_name becomes the primary key, so DynamoDB enforces uniqueness itself and no sentinel item or transaction is needed. option_id is kept as a plain attribute for lineage; DynamoDB has no auto-increment, so new options written after migration carry no option_id unless the application assigns one, and no in-scope query reads it.

trade_offs.description: option_value (LONGTEXT) stays inline in the item: the measured average row is 360 bytes against the 400 KB item limit, and capacity is sized on the 1,283-byte schema estimate that counts the column at 1 KB.
trade_offs.impact: A single option value larger than about 390 KB cannot be stored in one item. The write path stores such a value in Amazon S3 and writes the S3 object key in option_value with a marker, and the read path follows it; the migration checks MAX(LENGTH(option_value)) and moves any oversized row the same way.

trade_offs.description: Option reads use eventually consistent GetItem at 0.5 read unit per item, which keeps the read load at 1,289 read units per second at design rate.
trade_offs.impact: A GetItem issued right after an update_option returns the previous value until DynamoDB replicates the write to the replica serving the read, within about one second. Callers that must see their own write in the same request set ConsistentRead=true on that GetItem, at twice the read cost.

trade_offs.description: The hot-partition check assumes the whole read load lands on one option name: 1,289 read units per second is 43% of the 3,000 per-key limit, and 258 write units per second is 25.8% of the 1,000 per-key limit.
trade_offs.impact: Even if a single option such as the site URL receives every read, the key stays under the limit at ten times today's traffic. If one option's reads grow past 2,400 read units per second, put an ElastiCache cache in front of the option reads, as WordPress object caching already does.

trade_offs.description: No index on autoload is created, because no in-scope query filters on it; the source's autoload index is dropped.
trade_offs.impact: Loading all autoloaded options at once (the WordPress bootstrap query on autoload) is not in the observed workload. If that query is added, it needs a GSI keyed on autoload, sharded because the column has a handful of values, or a single cached bundle item maintained on write.

trade_offs.description: [PE note] Cost: on demand at design load, reads come to about 1,289 read units/s (~3.3B a month) and writes to about 258 write units/s (~670M a month). That is several hundred dollars a month, well over the $100 per-table threshold. Traffic is steady key-value traffic, so the team should compare provisioned capacity with auto scaling (or reserved capacity) against on-demand pricing.

MySQL's ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE only touches the listed columns. If option_id lineage matters, use UpdateItem SET option_value, autoload (it upserts too) instead of PutItem. No in-scope query reads option_id, so this is optional.

Reads must still check expiry, because TTL deletion can lag.

A caching layer in front of option reads that also caches misses (as WordPress object caching already does) would cut both cost and the load on any single key.

trade_offs.description: [PE note] MySQL reports 0 affected rows when an UPDATE sets a value identical to the current one. DynamoDB's conditional UpdateItem succeeds in that case. Callers that branch on the affected-row count should not depend on that MySQL behavior.

trade_offs.description: Option lookups by name are cached with negative entries. Query `66c96f95` returns a row on 28% of calls and query `e223aefb` on 8%, so a missing option is stored as __missing=1 instead of being skipped.
trade_offs.impact: About 72% of the 76 option reads per second, and most of the 10 autoload checks per second, are answered by the cache without touching Aurora MySQL. A newly created option is visible once the owner write's version bump and delete run, and after at most the one-hour TTL if that transaction fails.

trade_offs.description: Every read-then-fill key has a version key in its slot. Fills go through a Lua compare-and-set script, and writers bump the version in the same transaction that deletes the data keys.
trade_offs.impact: A reader that loaded stock=12 from Aurora MySQL before a checkout decremented it to 11 cannot write 12 back, because its fill is rejected once the version changes. A cache miss costs one extra GET and runs one script instead of a plain HSET. Version keys add about 500,000 small keys at 10x volume.

trade_offs.description: Post meta is cached per post as one hash, plus a second hash from meta_key to meta_id. Both are filled by one atomic script from one owner read, and any meta write deletes both.
trade_offs.impact: Five read shapes on wp_postmeta (about 32 reads per second) become single-key reads. Memory holds each post's meta twice (about 4.8 KB per post). A stock change deletes the whole post's meta cache. The fill lock then sends one reader, not every concurrent reader, to reload about 30 rows from Aurora MySQL.

trade_offs.description: Hash field order does not follow meta_id or order_item_id, so the client sorts the HGETALL result numerically to match the ORDER BY of the source queries.
trade_offs.impact: Sorting 10 to 30 fields in application code costs microseconds. Code that relied on database order calls the shared cache helper that sorts the fields.

trade_offs.description: Hashes that cache one field per query variant set their TTL only on the first fill (EXPIRE NX). Termmeta-ordered term lists carry a global termmeta version in the field name.
trade_offs.impact: A busy parent or object with new variants arriving still expires 10 minutes after its first fill, so the 10-minute limit holds. A termmeta write retires every older ordered list at once. Hot parents are rebuilt from Aurora MySQL every 10 minutes even when nothing changed.

trade_offs.description: The object-term joins (queries `d5ae7abb` and `4481cc0c`) are pre-joined into a term_id list per object, and the term rows are stored separately in wp_terms:{term_id}.
trade_offs.impact: About 16 join queries per second become one hash read per object. No captured write covers term assignment, so the term-assignment code path bumps the object's version and deletes its key.

trade_offs.description: Child and title lookups on wp_posts store only post IDs, cached per parent or per type and title. Empty results are cached too, because the child and title queries return 0 rows on average.
trade_offs.impact: Each lookup costs one key read plus pipelined row reads. The post write path computes the old and new parent and title and invalidates those keys, which is extra application code for each post save.

trade_offs.description: The slug uniqueness check, query `fcfd82fa`, stays on Aurora MySQL and is not cached.
trade_offs.impact: Its 2.7 calls per second still reach Aurora MySQL through the post_name index. In exchange, no stale cache entry can produce a duplicate slug, which matters because wp_posts has no unique constraint on post_name.

trade_offs.description: Action scheduler reads use a 60-second TTL because the scheduler's status, claim and attempt updates are absent from the captured write set. Hook lookups cache only two fixed status sets and at most 1,000 actions per hook, with zero-padded members so equal scores sort by numeric action_id.
trade_offs.impact: An action's cached status lags the database by up to 60 seconds when the scheduler's update path does not invalidate the key. Claiming and running actions read and write Aurora MySQL directly, so the cache never decides whether an action runs. Hooks with more than 1,000 matching actions, and other status lists, read Aurora MySQL.

trade_offs.description: WooCommerce order items and item meta are cached per order and per item, with a meta_key-to-meta_id companion hash for existence checks. Invalidation also covers item updates, item deletes and meta deletes made outside the captured workload.
trade_offs.impact: About 22 order reads per second are served by the cache. A removed line item or meta row disappears from the cache when its write path runs the invalidation transaction, and after at most the 30-minute TTL if that fails. Checkout and payment reads that need the committed state read Aurora MySQL.

trade_offs.description: Tax rate classes (2 rows) are one pre-sorted JSON string with a 24-hour TTL, and no captured write covers the table.
trade_offs.impact: A tax class edit is visible after the admin save path invalidates the key, and after at most 24 hours if that path is missing.

trade_offs.description: Key counts in the key designs are already 10x today's rows: 11,990 posts become 119,900 post keys, 23,163 options become 231,630 option keys and 24,713 order items become 247,130 item meta keys. At that 10x volume the cache holds about 1.7 million data keys plus about 0.5 million version keys and about 1.4 GB of values. Adding per-key overhead of about 90 B (about 0.2 GB) and hashtable encoding for meta hashes whose JSON values exceed the 64 B hash-max-listpack-value (about 0.7 GB) gives about 2.3 GB.
trade_offs.impact: The cluster runs in cluster mode with 2 shards. Each shard is one cache.r7g.large primary and one replica, at 13.07 GiB per node. With reserved-memory-percent 25 that leaves about 19.6 GiB of usable data memory, which holds the 2.3 GB 10x estimate with about 8x headroom. It also holds the 14 GB figure that results if the per-key counts are read as today's volume. The parameter group sets maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru for the whole cluster. Oversized values always read Aurora MySQL.

trade_offs.description: Key patterns use literal hash tags. The braces in wp_postmeta:{post_id} hold the actual post_id, so a data key, its :keys companion, its :ver key and its :lock key share one slot.
trade_offs.impact: Fills and invalidations for one entity run as a single script or MULTI under cluster mode. A post save that touches several parents or titles sends one small transaction per slot in a pipeline. Each one is idempotent and is retried on its own.

trade_offs.description: Values over 100 KB are cached as an __oversize=1 marker with the normal TTL instead of being skipped, and autoloaded options are held in the PHP process for 5 seconds.
trade_offs.impact: A large serialized option or post costs one small cache read and one direct Aurora MySQL read, with no failed fill attempt. Autoloaded options read on every page skip the network round trip, and stay stale for at most 5 seconds after an option change.

trade_offs.description: [PE note] In cluster mode, IN-list reads (EC-AP-2, EC-AP-3, EC-AP-14) span slots. The client has to use a cluster-aware pipeline that splits commands by slot. The Aurora fill must read each missing entity's `:ver` before the single owner query.

trade_offs.description: [PE note] Numeric IDs share hash tags across tables: `wp_posts:{1842}`, `wp_postmeta:{1842}`, `wp_term_relationships:{1842}` and `wp_actionscheduler_actions:{1842}` all land in the same slot. That is harmless for overall distribution, but a viral product concentrates all of its keys on one shard. Watch per-shard EngineCPUUtilization.

unsupported_patterns.reason: This is the slug uniqueness check WordPress runs while saving a post. wp_posts has no unique index on (post_type, post_name), so this query is the only thing preventing duplicate slugs. A cache hit that missed a concurrent insert or a failed delete would produce duplicate slugs and URL collisions. The query runs only on post save (2.7 calls per second), so caching it saves little load.
unsupported_patterns.workaround: Run the check on Aurora MySQL against the existing post_name index, inside the post save path. The cache does not hold or answer slug lookups.

migration_notes.application_logic_required: Deleting a key after commit does not stop a reader that queried Aurora MySQL before the write from writing the old value back afterwards. Every read-then-fill key is therefore guarded by a version key in its slot. Readers GET {data_key}:ver before the Aurora MySQL query and fill only through the versioned fill script, which compares the version and writes the hash, any companion hash and the TTL atomically. Writers run MULTI, INCR the version key, EXPIRE it, DEL the data keys, EXEC after commit.

After a post insert, update or delete commits, the application reads the old and new post_parent, post_type and post_title. It then runs a version bump and DEL for wp_posts:{ID}, both children keys and both title keys. Those keys sit in different slots, so this is one small MULTI per slot sent in one pipeline, and each MULTI is idempotent and retried on failure.

After any postmeta or order item meta write commits, including the `meta_value + ?` and `meta_value - ?` stock updates, the application bumps the entity's version and deletes the meta hash and its :keys hash in one MULTI on the entity's slot.

migration_notes.object_name: delete paths outside the captured workload
migration_notes.application_logic_required: The application adds the versioned invalidation transaction to these paths: delete_post_meta (postmeta keys), wp_delete_post (post, meta, children and title keys), wc_update_order_item and wc_delete_order_item (the parent order's items key, plus the item's meta and :keys hashes on delete), and order item meta deletes.

The scheduler's claim, status and attempt updates are not in the captured workload. Its data store layer runs a version bump and DEL on wp_actionscheduler_actions:{action_id} and on the hook's two status-set keys after each update. Claim and execution logic keeps reading Aurora MySQL.

The cache client writes __missing=1 for absent options, __loaded=1 for filled meta and item hashes, the member 0 with score -1 for empty action sets, __oversize=1 for options, posts and post meta over 100 KB, and the member __oversize with score -2 for hooks with more than 1,000 actions. It treats __missing, __loaded and the empty sentinel as authoritative no-row answers, and sends __oversize reads straight to Aurora MySQL without trying a fill.

migration_notes.object_name: term assignment, term edits and termmeta ordering
migration_notes.application_logic_required: No term relationship or term taxonomy writes were captured. The term-assignment path bumps the version of wp_term_relationships:{object_id} and deletes it. Term edits and count updates do the same for wp_terms:{term_id}. Termmeta writes INCR wp_termmeta:ver, and readers include that value in the orderby_meta field name.
wp_posts has no unique constraint on post_name, so the slug check in the post save path stays on Aurora MySQL and is never answered from the cache.

On a miss for options, posts, post meta and item meta, the reader runs SET {data_key}:lock 1 NX PX 2000. Only the lock holder queries Aurora MySQL and fills. Other readers sleep 25 ms and reread up to 4 times, then read Aurora MySQL without filling. Autoloaded options (siteurl, home, active_plugins and the rest of autoload=yes) are held in the PHP process cache for 5 seconds. Option reads can use replicas (READONLY in cluster mode).

The fill script uses EXPIRE with the NX flag, which needs ElastiCache for Valkey 7.2 or later (or Redis OSS 7.0 or later). On Valkey 9.0 or later, per-field HEXPIRE can replace whole-key TTLs on the variant hashes. The cluster parameter group sets maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru and reserved-memory-percent 25 for the whole cluster.

trade_offs.description: The source index type_status_date leads with ID, so it cannot serve filters on post_type and post_status. The target redefines it as (post_type, post_status, post_date, ID), the column order WordPress core defines.

Query `12f856ea` excludes statuses with `!=`, so it still scans every row of its post type and sorts them: rows examined drop from about 15,790 per call to about the row count of that post type, and a filesort remains. trade_offs.description: Composite indexes are added on wp_postmeta (post_id, meta_key) and wp_woocommerce_order_itemmeta (order_item_id, meta_key), and on wp_actionscheduler_actions (hook, group_id, status, claim_id). The single-column indexes stay because they return rows already ordered by meta_id for the per-object meta loads.
trade_offs.impact: Meta lookups by object and key read one row instead of 10 to 19 rows, and the WooCommerce sales reports join meta by key without scanning. Each insert into these tables maintains one more index, which costs little at the observed near-zero write rate. Storage grows by a few tens of MB.

trade_offs.description: Reporting queries go to an Aurora Replica through the reader endpoint, and repeated option, meta and term reads go to an ElastiCache object cache. The schema stays a 1:1 carry-over of the WordPress and WooCommerce tables.
trade_offs.impact: Report results on the replica can trail the writer by up to about 100 ms of replica lag, which does not affect sales totals shown in dashboards. Keeping the WordPress schema unchanged means plugins and core upgrades keep working with no code changes.

trade_offs.impact: Drafts keep their floating publish dates and WordPress behaves after cutover exactly as before. trade_offs.description: The last_access update (query `0452bed2`, 248.3 calls per second at design load, 46.68% lock time in MySQL) is throttled in the application: it writes only when the key's last written last_access is more than 60 s old, using the per-key value cached in ElastiCache and the last_access now projected into ApiKeysByConsumerKey.
trade_offs.impact: DynamoDB receives at most one write per API key per 60 s, bounded at 3.88 writes per second table-wide (the 1.56% of source calls that change a row) for 7.76 WCU/s instead of 496.6 WCU/s, a 64x cut that also removes the single-item worst case (0.8% of one partition's write limit instead of 49.7%). Because last_access is now projected, each real write also writes ApiKeysByConsumerKey once (7.76 WCU/s), which stays rare under the throttle. The access pattern keeps the 248.3 calls per second as its design rate because that is the measured call rate; the hot partition entries carry the throttled write rate. Row-lock waits disappear because each DynamoDB write is atomic per item, and last_access is at most 60 s behind the latest request, matching the source where 98% of updates change no row.

trade_offs.description: API key authentication by consumer_key (query `1794daed`) reads the ApiKeysByConsumerKey GSI with an INCLUDE projection of user_id, permissions, consumer_secret, nonces and last_access, so the lookup needs no base-table fetch.
trade_offs.impact: ApiKeysByConsumerKey lags the WpWoocommerceApiKeys table until DynamoDB applies each write to it; a request using a key created in that window fails authentication, and the key-creation flow that must use the key at once reads the base item by key_id with a strongly consistent GetItem. consumer_key is not unique in the source, so no uniqueness sentinel is written.

trade_offs.description: The full table scan of tax rate classes (query `329367a2`, 37.9 reads per second) becomes one Query on a single TAX_RATE_CLASS item collection whose sort key is the class name followed by its id.
trade_offs.impact: The 2-item list comes back in name order from one partition for 18.95 RCU/s, 0.6% of the partition limit. The unique slug is set only by the migration (no in-scope write changes it), so no sentinel item is needed; an admin flow that adds classes later writes a slug sentinel with attribute_not_exists in the same transaction. ElastiCache can hold the list if read volume grows further.

trade_offs.description: DynamoDB has no server-side COUNT, so the approved-comment count per post (query `8c66eaee`) is served in scope by a KEYS_ONLY GSI CommentsByPostApproval (comment_post_id, comment_approved) queried with Select=COUNT instead of a maintained counter item.
trade_offs.impact: Each count reads every matching index entry; the source examines 2.4 rows per call, so a count reads 2.4 index entries for 0.5 RCU. A counter item was not chosen because approval status changes happen in writes outside this workload, and a counter updated only on insert would drift. comment_approved is a mutable GSI key: each moderation change deletes and reinserts the index entry (2 index writes of 77 bytes). The count lags new comments until DynamoDB applies the write to the index.

trade_offs.description: Reserved stock and download permissions are keyed by order_id with the product_id or permission_id as sort key, so the delete by order (query `77cd1ad7`) and the customer reassignment by order (query `2264704d`) read their items by key.
trade_offs.impact: Each set-based statement becomes a Query on the order's items followed by a BatchWriteItem of deletes or one UpdateItem per permission. These are not atomic across items: a failed item is retried by the application, and both operations are idempotent, so a retry is safe.

trade_offs.description: Auto-increment ids (comment_ID, log_id, meta_id) have no DynamoDB equivalent; the application generates them (a time-ordered numeric id) and writes with attribute_not_exists on the key.
trade_offs.impact: Inserts no longer depend on a central sequence. Action scheduler logs are grouped per action_id with log_id as sort key, so the log of one action reads in time order.

trade_offs.description: Posts and post meta stay separate tables even though the analysis groups them, because no in-scope query reads them together: post reads fetch only wp_posts rows and post meta traffic is writes only.
trade_offs.impact: Post meta writes (about 260 write units per second at design load) scale on their own table without touching post items. A future page render that needs a post and its meta issues a GetItem plus a Query.

trade_offs.description: Order items are stored under their order (partition key order_id, sort key order_item_id), and order item meta under its order_item_id.

trade_offs.description: DynamoDB has no AUTO_INCREMENT, so the application generates ID, meta_id, umeta_id, order_item_id and action_id before each insert, and every insert carries attribute_not_exists on its key.
trade_offs.impact: An id generator (a counter item updated with an atomic ADD, or a time-ordered unique id) replaces the database sequence. The conditional put rejects a duplicate id instead of overwriting an existing row.

trade_offs.description: The table is keyed by option_name instead of the auto-increment option_id, because every in-scope read and write addresses an option by name.
trade_offs.impact: Every query becomes a single-item GetItem, PutItem, UpdateItem or DeleteItem. The unique index on option_name becomes the primary key, so DynamoDB enforces uniqueness itself and no sentinel item or transaction is needed. option_id is kept as a plain attribute for lineage; DynamoDB has no auto-increment, so new options written after migration carry no option_id unless the application assigns one, and no in-scope query reads it.

trade_offs.description: option_value (LONGTEXT) stays inline in the item: the measured average row is 360 bytes against the 400 KB item limit, and capacity is sized on the 1,283-byte schema estimate that counts the column at 1 KB.
trade_offs.impact: A single option value larger than about 390 KB cannot be stored in one item. The write path stores such a value in Amazon S3 and writes the S3 object key in option_value with a marker, and the read path follows it; the migration checks MAX(LENGTH(option_value)) and moves any oversized row the same way.

trade_offs.description: Option reads use eventually consistent GetItem at 0.5 read unit per item, which keeps the read load at 1,289 read units per second at design rate.
trade_offs.impact: A GetItem issued right after an update_option returns the previous value until DynamoDB replicates the write to the replica serving the read, within about one second. Callers that must see their own write in the same request set ConsistentRead=true on that GetItem, at twice the read cost.

trade_offs.description: The hot-partition check assumes the whole read load lands on one option name: 1,289 read units per second is 43% of the 3,000 per-key limit, and 258 write units per second is 25.8% of the 1,000 per-key limit.
trade_offs.impact: Even if a single option such as the site URL receives every read, the key stays under the limit at ten times today's traffic. trade_offs.description: Option lookups by name are cached with negative entries. Query `66c96f95` returns a row on 28% of calls and query `e223aefb` on 8%, so a missing option is stored as __missing=1 instead of being skipped.
trade_offs.impact: About 72% of the 76 option reads per second, and most of the 10 autoload checks per second, are answered by the cache without touching Aurora MySQL. A newly created option is visible once the owner write's version bump and delete run, and after at most the one-hour TTL if that transaction fails.

trade_offs.description: Every read-then-fill key has a version key in its slot. Fills go through a Lua compare-and-set script, and writers bump the version in the same transaction that deletes the data keys.
trade_offs.impact: A reader that loaded stock=12 from Aurora MySQL before a checkout decremented it to 11 cannot write 12 back, because its fill is rejected once the version changes. A cache miss costs one extra GET and runs one script instead of a plain HSET. Version keys add about 500,000 small keys at 10x volume.

trade_offs.description: Post meta is cached per post as one hash, plus a second hash from meta_key to meta_id. Both are filled by one atomic script from one owner read, and any meta write deletes both.
trade_offs.impact: Five read shapes on wp_postmeta (about 32 reads per second) become single-key reads. Memory holds each post's meta twice (about 4.8 KB per post). A stock change deletes the whole post's meta cache. The fill lock then sends one reader, not every concurrent reader, to reload about 30 rows from Aurora MySQL.

trade_offs.description: Hash field order does not follow meta_id or order_item_id, so the client sorts the HGETALL result numerically to match the ORDER BY of the source queries.
trade_offs.impact: Sorting 10 to 30 fields in application code costs microseconds. Code that relied on database order calls the shared cache helper that sorts the fields.

trade_offs.description: Hashes that cache one field per query variant set their TTL only on the first fill (EXPIRE NX). Termmeta-ordered term lists carry a global termmeta version in the field name.
trade_offs.impact: A busy parent or object with new variants arriving still expires 10 minutes after its first fill, so the 10-minute limit holds. A termmeta write retires every older ordered list at once. Hot parents are rebuilt from Aurora MySQL every 10 minutes even when nothing changed.

trade_offs.description: The object-term joins (queries `d5ae7abb` and `4481cc0c`) are pre-joined into a term_id list per object, and the term rows are stored separately in wp_terms:{term_id}.
trade_offs.impact: About 16 join queries per second become one hash read per object. No captured write covers term assignment, so the term-assignment code path bumps the object's version and deletes its key.

trade_offs.description: Child and title lookups on wp_posts store only post IDs, cached per parent or per type and title. Empty results are cached too, because the child and title queries return 0 rows on average.
trade_offs.impact: Each lookup costs one key read plus pipelined row reads. The post write path computes the old and new parent and title and invalidates those keys, which is extra application code for each post save.

trade_offs.description: The slug uniqueness check, query `fcfd82fa`, stays on Aurora MySQL and is not cached.
trade_offs.impact: Its 2.7 calls per second still reach Aurora MySQL through the post_name index. In exchange, no stale cache entry can produce a duplicate slug, which matters because wp_posts has no unique constraint on post_name.

trade_offs.description: Action scheduler reads use a 60-second TTL because the scheduler's status, claim and attempt updates are absent from the captured write set. Hook lookups cache only two fixed status sets and at most 1,000 actions per hook, with zero-padded members so equal scores sort by numeric action_id.
trade_offs.impact: An action's cached status lags the database by up to 60 seconds when the scheduler's update path does not invalidate the key. Claiming and running actions read and write Aurora MySQL directly, so the cache never decides whether an action runs. Hooks with more than 1,000 matching actions, and other status lists, read Aurora MySQL.

trade_offs.description: WooCommerce order items and item meta are cached per order and per item, with a meta_key-to-meta_id companion hash for existence checks. Invalidation also covers item updates, item deletes and meta deletes made outside the captured workload.
trade_offs.impact: About 22 order reads per second are served by the cache. A removed line item or meta row disappears from the cache when its write path runs the invalidation transaction, and after at most the 30-minute TTL if that fails. Checkout and payment reads that need the committed state read Aurora MySQL.

trade_offs.description: Tax rate classes (2 rows) are one pre-sorted JSON string with a 24-hour TTL, and no captured write covers the table.
trade_offs.impact: A tax class edit is visible after the admin save path invalidates the key, and after at most 24 hours if that path is missing.

trade_offs.description: Key counts in the key designs are already 10x today's rows: 11,990 posts become 119,900 post keys, 23,163 options become 231,630 option keys and 24,713 order items become 247,130 item meta keys. At that 10x volume the cache holds about 1.7 million data keys plus about 0.5 million version keys and about 1.4 GB of values. Adding per-key overhead of about 90 B (about 0.2 GB) and hashtable encoding for meta hashes whose JSON values exceed the 64 B hash-max-listpack-value (about 0.7 GB) gives about 2.3 GB.
trade_offs.impact: The cluster runs in cluster mode with 2 shards. Each shard is one cache.r7g.large primary and one replica, at 13.07 GiB per node. With reserved-memory-percent 25 that leaves about 19.6 GiB of usable data memory, which holds the 2.3 GB 10x estimate with about 8x headroom. It also holds the 14 GB figure that results if the per-key counts are read as today's volume. The parameter group sets maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru for the whole cluster. Oversized values always read Aurora MySQL.

trade_offs.description: Key patterns use literal hash tags. The braces in wp_postmeta:{post_id} hold the actual post_id, so a data key, its :keys companion, its :ver key and its :lock key share one slot.
trade_offs.impact: Fills and invalidations for one entity run as a single script or MULTI under cluster mode. A post save that touches several parents or titles sends one small transaction per slot in a pipeline. Each one is idempotent and is retried on its own.

trade_offs.description: Values over 100 KB are cached as an __oversize=1 marker with the normal TTL instead of being skipped, and autoloaded options are held in the PHP process for 5 seconds.
trade_offs.impact: A large serialized option or post costs one small cache read and one direct Aurora MySQL read, with no failed fill attempt. Autoloaded options read on every page skip the network round trip, and stay stale for at most 5 seconds after an option change.

trade_offs.description: [PE note] In cluster mode, IN-list reads (EC-AP-2, EC-AP-3, EC-AP-14) span slots. The client has to use a cluster-aware pipeline that splits commands by slot. The Aurora fill must read each missing entity's `:ver` before the single owner query.
